title: Dabo Swinney says he doesn’t need another title to prove himself, has no plans to retire
content:
CHARLOTTE, N.C – With two national titles to his name, Clemson coach Dabo Swinney is past the point of trying to validate his worth.

“Well, most people don’t have one, and probably never will get one. So I don’t really feel like I gotta go win another national title to prove anything to anybody,” Swinney told The Athletic at ACC Kickoff on Thursday.

“I just wanna focus on the things that really drive me, and that is impacting these guys’ lives, truly fulfilling the purpose that we have in our program. Nobody wants to win more than me. And we’ve won 11 (conference and national) championships in the last 15 years. I think the next closest coach has six. So, being who I am, that’s served us well. So I don’t know how to be anything other than me, but as far as, like, I gotta go win another national championship to prove something to somebody, I’m not really wired that way.”

Swinney built a program at Clemson that went toe-to-toe with Nick Saban’s Alabama dynasty for half of the 2010s. The past five years haven’t been the same, and Clemson is coming off its worst season (7-6) under Swinney since 2010, his third year as head coach.

The 2025 team was one of the country’s biggest disappointments. Coming off a College Football Playoff appearance and with some highly touted returnees anchoring the defense, a return to national championship contention seemed possible for the Tigers.

Instead, Clemson finished tied for seventh in the ACC with a 4-4 record, including home losses to Syracuse, Duke and SMU.

“Because we were terrible in pass defense, the worst I’ve had,” Swinney said of last year’s team. “And we didn’t run the ball anywhere near like we need to, which affected us on third down, affected our scoring.”

When the NFL Draft rolled around in April, Clemson’s missed opportunity seemed even more glaring. The Tigers had nine players drafted, including two in the first round. Quarterback Cade Klubnik went in the fourth round to the New York Jets.

“I don’t think you want to dwell on that, but at the same time, you don’t want to completely forget it because there are many aspects of not only the game of football, but the game of life that you can learn from a season like that last year,” said linebacker Sammy Brown, sounding a bit like his coach. “How to overcome adversity, how to be a man and face adversity and be able to overcome it.’

“At the end of the day, we really are focusing this offseason on resetting and, you know, resetting our goals, resetting our standards and learning from last year, but this is a new season, this is a new team.”

Clemson will be breaking in a new starter at quarterback for the first time since 2023. While Swinney has become more active in the transfer portal, he’s riding with in-house options this season. Chris Vizzina Jr., entering his fourth season in the program with 105 career pass attempts, is the presumptive starter, though freshman Tait Reynolds has already made his presence felt.

Swinney also turned back the clock, rehiring Chad Morris as offensive coordinator after parting ways with Garrett Riley. Morris was at Clemson from 2011 to ‘14, helping Swinney launch one of the most successful runs in college football history.

“Everybody compares us to ‘15-19,” Swinney said, referring to the stretch in which the Tigers went 69-5, made the four-team CFP four times and won national titles in 2016 and ‘18, beating Saban’s Crimson Tide each time. “They say that but don’t have perspective. That was the winningest five years in college football. It’s been done once. So if that’s always what you’re gonna be compared to, you’re gonna have a lot of failure.”

Clemson is 57-22 since, with two more Playoff appearances but no CFP victories.

“The arrow’s kind of going the wrong way based on some recent stuff we’ve done this past year, but it’s our job to get it turned around and headed back toward the top,” Swinney said.

Like every coach in the sport, Swinney looks around at the rapidly changing world of college sports and sees “chaos.”

“It’s like a ship drifting out to sea,” Swinney said. “Nobody’s navigating it. It’s waiting for somebody to point it somewhere. It’s just kind of floating around.”

Swinney said he’s still motivated by charting a course through that uncertainty for the Tigers, even if he feels his personal legacy needs no validation.

“I love the challenge of trying to figure this out,” he said. “We’ve been affected at Clemson, but on a scale of 1-10 we’re like a 3 based on what I’ve seen at a lot of these places out there.”

Swinney has some ideas to fix the sport as a whole but said he’s more focused on doing the job he’s paid to do.

“I can’t save the world so I don’t even worry about it. I just focus on Clemson,” he said. “Listen, Clemson ain’t ever been in a better spot. Culturally, programatically, yeah we didn’t have a good season last year, but our culture, we lead the nation in graduation, lead the nation in retention in an era where they can leave any time they want.

“The kids love it there. They stay there. We don’t have a lot of issues and we’ve won.”

Swinney is also quick to point out that if championships are the ultimate measure of success, he’s still doing better than most of his peers.

“How many teams have won championships?” he said. “There’s a lot of coaches that get paid a lot of money. They get paid to win and they ain’t ever won. The money I get paid is because we won. Ain’t nobody give me nothing. We’ve had to earn it.”

While Swinney is not out to prove anything, he is not lacking motivation or enthusiasm for the job of making Clemson the best it can be: “I love the place I’m at. I love who I’m with. I love the kids. I love the game. I’m just getting going. Some people say, ‘Is he gonna retire?’ Retire? And do what? I’m a football coach.”

He made note that at 56, he is the same age Saban was when he was hired by Alabama.

“He coached until he was 73,” Swinney said. “I ain’t coaching until I’m 73. But I got a lot more to do.”
